appraisal_events.evidence: "Comme tu as l'air fatigué et agité" ; "les regards de Robert semblaient par moments atteindre à une profondeur qu'ils quittaient aussitôt comme un plongeur qui a touché le fond... c'était l'idée qu'il avait rompu avec sa maîtresse" ; "c'est bon de voir son petit garçon" ; "cette tendresse paraissant agacer Robert".
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator confirms and deepens the mother's public diagnosis ("Et en effet"), showing Robert visibly worn and secretly wounded by the rupture, then has him publicly infantilized as "son petit garçon" and led off to the back of the salon. The narration is sympathetic rather than mocking, but its dominant local movement lowers Robert.

appraisal_events.evidence: "Mme Swann se trouvant seule et ayant compris que j'étais lié avec Saint-Loup me fit signe de venir auprès d'elle."
appraisal_events.explanation: Mme Swann, cold to the narrator moments earlier, now summons him to her side once she grasps his connection with Saint-Loup; his local inclusion rises on the strength of that association rather than on his own account.

status_effects.explanation: Robert is locally at his weakest: the rupture with his mistress is a wound he can only touch and flee, and his agitation is legible to everyone in the salon.
Being petted, called "son petit garçon" and steered away by his mother in front of the assembled guests reduces him locally from a man of the world to a child.
He moves from being kept at a chilly distance to being explicitly beckoned into Mme Swann's company, admitted through his link to Saint-Loup.

ambiguities: Mme Swann's summons is reported without comment, but its stated cause (her realizing he is close with Saint-Loup) makes the warmth visibly instrumental; the passage leaves open whether this is plain report or quiet irony at her expense, which is why the event is scored as gain for the narrator rather than as any credit to her.
